warmup.q: Six machines each take one random place on a ring of hash values, and each owns the stretch of ring that ends at its place, like the six friends and their pizza. Roughly how much of the ring does the luckiest machine own?
options: About 17%, a sixth: random places come out fair
About 20%: a little luck either way
About 40%: six random cuts leave some very long gaps
It depends on how many payments you store
warmup.why: A hash spreads thousands of keys evenly, but six machine places are only six random points, and six random cuts of a circle are very uneven. With S machines, the longest stretch is on average (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/S) / S of the ring, about 41% for six. The first section's demo measures 44.0%. The last option tempts anyone who has seen keys spread well: the share depends on where the machines sit, and the keys only fill it in.

sections.h: A ring of hash values, and why one place per machine is unfair
sections.html:
Splitting data: key ranges, hashes and tenants picked a payment's shard with hash mod N. Hash the key, which turns it into a big random-looking number, then keep the remainder after dividing by N. That spreads keys evenly until N changes. Going from 4 machines to 5 moves 80% of the keys. A key stays put only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 4 and for 5. In any 20 numbers in a row, that's true for only 4 of them. (From here on we write S for the number of machines, or nodes, because N will mean the number of copies of each key, as in the Replication track.)

Consistent hashing is the fix that Cassandra, a free database program built to spread over many machines, is built on. It comes from Dynamo, Amazon's 2007 design for such a store. Lay every possible hash value around a circle, like the edge of the pizza. That circle is the ring. Each node sits at the hash of its own name, and that place is its token: the node's cut in the pizza. Each key sits at the hash of the key and belongs to the first node you meet walking clockwise. So a node owns the arc, the stretch of ring, that ends at its token. A new node takes only the keys on the arc just before its token, from one neighbour, and no other key moves. That's what "consistent" means here: most keys stay where they were when the nodes change. It has nothing to do with consistent data.

This first version of the ring, with one token per node, has a flaw of its own. The ring demo in Why other data models exist: Bigtable, Dynamo and the families put six nodes on a ring with one token each. Node-E ended up owning 44.6% of the ring, and node-D 5%. That wasn't bad luck. It's what one random place per node does.

A good hash is as good as random, and random points on a circle don't spread out evenly. They clump in some places and leave long gaps in others, like the friends' cuts. With S nodes, the longest gap is on average (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/S) / S of the ring. For six nodes that's about 41%, where a fair share is 16.7%. The node at the end of that gap holds 41% of the keys, stores 41% of the data and answers 41% of the requests, while its neighbour sits nearly idle. Buying a seventh machine doesn't fix it, because the new token lands at random too.

It gets worse when nodes come and go. A node that joins takes whatever arc its token lands in, all of it from one neighbour. A node that dies hands its whole arc to the next node clockwise, which can double that node's work at the worst moment. Dynamo's paper names the problem, "non-uniform data and load distribution", and a second one: one token per node can't say that one machine is bigger than another.

Version 2 gives every node many tokens, which Dynamo calls virtual nodes. Node A takes T tokens, at the hashes of node-A#0, node-A#1 and so on, and owns T small arcs scattered round the ring. At the pizza, each friend makes 16 thin cuts instead of one. A node's share is the sum of its arcs, and a sum of many random pieces lands much closer to its average than one piece does. The demo below measures six nodes. With one token each, the biggest share is 44.0%. With 64 it's 18.6%, and with 256 it's 17.4%, against a fair 16.7%.

The improvement isn't smooth. Sixteen random tokens still leave one node at 24.3%, worse than four tokens did. Random placement is noisy when T is small, which is why Cassandra doesn't place its 16 tokens at random, as the third section shows. Tokens fix the bigger-machine problem too: give a machine with twice the capacity twice the tokens.

Each node owns many small arcs scattered round one ring, and a key belongs to the arc it lands in. Joining, leaving, copies and busy keys, the rest of this lesson, are all questions about those arcs. Next, we'll add a node and watch which arcs change hands.

try.title: Measure the shares with 1 to 256 tokens per node
steps: Read RingBalanceDemo.kt. It builds the ring as a TreeMap, Java's sorted map, from token to node, with T tokens per node at the MD5 hash of node-A#0, node-A#1 and so on. Then it adds up the arc before each token. No Docker needed.
Predict: with 16 tokens per node, will the biggest share be closer to 44% or to the fair 16.7%?

code.title: RingBalanceDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l02.demo import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.TreeMap /** Where text lands on a ring of 2^64 positions: the first 8 bytes of its MD5. */ fun position(text: String): Long = ByteBuffer.wrap(MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(text.toByteArray())).long /** A ring with [tokensPerNode] tokens for each node: token position -> node. */ fun ring(nodes: List<String>, tokensPerNode: Int): TreeMap<Long, String> { val tokens = TreeMap<Long, String>() for (node in nodes) for (i in 0 until tokensPerNode) tokens[position("$node#$i")] = node return tokens } /** Each node's share of the ring: the gap before each of its tokens, summed. */ fun shares(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>): Map<String, Double> { val share = sortedMapOf<String, Double>() var previous = tokens.lastKey() for ((token, node) in tokens) { share[node] = (share[node] ?: 0.0) + (token - previous).toULong().toDouble() / 18446744073709551616.0 previous = token } return share } /** Six nodes, the same names as the ring demo in the Data models track's first lesson. How even is the ring with 1, 4, 16, 64 and 256 tokens each? */ fun main() { val nodes = listOf("node-A", "node-B", "node-C", "node-D", "node-E", "node-F") println("one token per node:") shares(ring(nodes, 1)).forEach { (node, share) -> println(" %s owns %5.1f%%".format(node, share * 100)) } println("tokens per node smallest share largest share largest / fair (16.7%)") for (t in listOf(1, 4, 16, 64, 256)) { val s = shares(ring(nodes, t)).values println("%15d %13.1f%% %12.1f%% %20.2f".format(t, s.min() * 100, s.max() * 100, s.max() * nodes.size)) } }

try.expect:
one token per node:
  node-A owns  13.6%
  node-B owns  26.1%
  node-C owns   1.6%
  node-D owns   7.9%
  node-E owns  44.0%
  node-F owns   6.8%
tokens per node   smallest share   largest share   largest / fair (16.7%)
              1             1.6%           44.0%                   2.64
              4            12.8%           23.4%                   1.40
             16             9.3%           24.3%                   1.46
             64            15.2%           18.6%                   1.12
            256            16.1%           17.4%                   1.04

You get exactly these numbers, because MD5 gives the same hash on every computer. With one token, node-E owns 44.0% and node-C 1.6%, a 27-fold spread. Many tokens pull every node toward 16.7%, but not smoothly: 16 random tokens came out slightly worse than 4. Random placement only evens out with a large T, and that's the cost Cassandra's token allocator avoids. (The shares differ from the Data models track's demo because the tokens here are the hashes of node-A#0 and so on, not of node-A.)

video.title: Consistent hashing: why adding a node moves few keys

sections.h: A new machine joins, and takes keys from the nodes beside its tokens
sections.html:
Adding a node isn't free. Before it can answer for its keys, their data has to be copied to it from the nodes that held them, while those nodes keep serving card payments. Filling a new node like this is called bootstrapping, and in Dynamo's first design it took almost a day during the busy shopping season. So it matters how much moves, and who has to send it.

With one token per node, the new node takes one arc from one node. In the demo below, node-E joins four nodes, and its token lands inside node-D's long arc. E takes 43,894 of 100,000 keys, every one of them from D. One machine copies 44% of the data on its own. The hash mod S of the last lesson would have moved 80,221 keys and shuffled them among all five nodes, so the ring is still far better. But one unlucky token decides who does all the work.

With 16 tokens per node, E's 16 tokens land in 16 places, and each takes the slice just before it from whoever owned it. In the demo, 17,842 keys move: 6,997 from A, 5,576 from B and 5,269 from D. Three machines each send a slice at the same time. C happened to lose nothing. The stepper shows both joins.

Leaving runs the same film backwards. When a node with 16 tokens dies, each of its arcs falls to the next token clockwise, and those tokens belong to many different nodes. Dynamo's paper says a failed node's load "is evenly dispersed across the remaining available nodes". With one token per node, one neighbour inherits all of it.

The ring isn't the only way to get there. Two designs need no ring at all, and still move about 1/S of the keys, all to the new node. Rendezvous hashing, also called highest random weight (Thaler and Ravishankar, 1996), scores every node for each key with hash(key + node) and gives the key to the highest score. A new node wins about 1/S of the keys, taken evenly from every old node. The price is S hashes for every lookup. Jump consistent hash (Lamping and Veach, Google, 2014) is a loop of about five lines. It turns a key into a bucket number from 0 to S - 1, with no table and no tokens. Its catch is the numbering: you can only add or remove the last bucket. That suits numbered shards whose copies cover for failures. It doesn't suit a group of cache servers where any one of them can die. The Try it runs both next to the ring.

Copies need one more rule. A key is stored on N nodes, the first N you meet walking clockwise from the key, as Why other data models exist described. With virtual nodes, the next few tokens often belong to the same machine, and two copies on one machine protect nothing, because they die together. So the walk skips any token whose node is already on the list, until it has N different machines. Dynamo calls that list the key's preference list, and the lab's preferenceList builds it the same way.

Next, we'll leave the model and read the tokens off a real cluster.

try.title: Count what moves when node-E joins
steps: Read RingJoinDemo.kt. It places 100,000 payment keys on four nodes, adds node-E, and counts the keys whose owner changed, and who gave them up. It does this for hash mod S, for a ring with one token per node and with 16, and for jump hash and rendezvous hashing.
Predict which one moves the most keys, and which ones take keys from all four old nodes.

code.title: RingJoinDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l02.demo /** Jump consistent hash (Lamping and Veach, 2014): a key's bucket from 0 until [buckets], with no table at all. */ fun jumpHash(key: Long, buckets: Int): Int { var k = key var b = -1L var j = 0L while (j < buckets) { b = j k = k * 2862933555777941757L + 1 // a 64-bit linear congruential step: a new pseudo-random k j = ((b + 1) * ((1L shl 31).toDouble() / ((k ushr 33) + 1).toDouble())).toLong() // the next bucket this key jumps to } return b.toInt() } /** Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing: score every node for this key and take the highest. */ fun rendezvous(key: String, nodes: List<String>): String = nodes.maxBy { position("$key|$it") } /** A fifth node joins four. Which keys move, and where do they come from? */ fun main() { val four = listOf("node-A", "node-B", "node-C", "node-D") val five = four + "node-E" val keys = (0 until 100_000).map { "pay-$it" } // lesson 1's placement: node number hash mod S fun modOwner(key: String, nodes: List<String>) = nodes[Math.floorMod(position(key), nodes.size.toLong()).toInt()] val modMoved = keys.count { modOwner(it, four) != modOwner(it, five) } println("hash mod S, 4 -> 5 nodes: %,d of %,d keys move".format(modMoved, keys.size)) for (t in listOf(1, 16)) { val before = ring(four, t) val after = ring(five, t) // the owner is the node of the first token at or after the key; past the top, wrap to the first fun owner(tokens: java.util.TreeMap<Long, String>, key: String) = (tokens.ceilingEntry(position(key)) ?: tokens.firstEntry()).value val moved = keys.filter { owner(before, it) != owner(after, it) } val gaveUp = moved.groupingBy { owner(before, it) }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("ring, %2d token(s) per node: %,d keys move, all to node-E; given up by %s".format(t, moved.size, gaveUp)) } // no ring: jump hash numbers the nodes 0 to 4, rendezvous scores all of them val jumpMoved = keys.filter { jumpHash(position(it), 4) != jumpHash(position(it), 5) } val jumpGaveUp = jumpMoved.groupingBy { four[jumpHash(position(it), 4)] }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("jump hash: %,d keys move, all to node-E; given up by %s".format(jumpMoved.size, jumpGaveUp)) val hrwMoved = keys.filter { rendezvous(it, four) != rendezvous(it, five) } val hrwGaveUp = hrwMoved.groupingBy { rendezvous(it, four) }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("rendezvous: %,d keys move, all to node-E; given up by %s".format(hrwMoved.size, hrwGaveUp)) }

try.expect:
hash mod S, 4 -> 5 nodes: 80,221 of 100,000 keys move
ring,  1 token(s) per node: 43,894 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-D=43894}
ring, 16 token(s) per node: 17,842 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-A=6997, node-B=5576, node-D=5269}
jump hash:               19,792 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-A=4991, node-B=5019, node-C=4895, node-D=4887}
rendezvous:              19,897 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-A=5051, node-B=4880, node-C=4967, node-D=4999}

hash mod S reshuffles 80% of the keys between every pair of nodes. On the ring, every key that moves goes to node-E, and no other node trades. With one token, all 43,894 come from node-D, whose arc node-E landed in. With 16 tokens, node-E takes about a fifth of the ring (17.8%), from three different nodes; node-C happened to give nothing. Jump hash and rendezvous both move almost exactly the fair fifth, about 5,000 keys from each old node, with no tokens at all.

sections.h: Cassandra's real ring: Murmur3 tokens, sixteen per node
sections.html:
Cassandra shows you its tokens, so let's look at a real ring. Its ring is every 64-bit number, from -2^63 to 2^63 - 1, about 18 billion billion places, half of them negative. Each node's settings file, cassandra.yaml, names the hash that puts keys on the ring: partitioner: org.apache.cassandra.dht.Murmur3Partitioner. Murmur3 is a fast hash made for spreading keys, not for keeping secrets. CQL, Cassandra's query language, shows you the result: SELECT token(account_id) turns A-1001 into -4994511478997274402. Every Cassandra cluster in the world computes the same number for that key, because the token depends only on the key.

How many tokens does a node get? The cassandra.yaml in the cassandra:5.0.9 image, the package Docker starts Cassandra from, says num_tokens: 16 and allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor: 3. The Cassandra docs tell the history. Releases before 3.0 picked tokens at random, so they needed 256 per node to even things out. Cassandra 3.0 added a token allocator. It picks a joining node's tokens on purpose, to balance the load for a given replication factor (RF). That's the number of copies of each row, the N of the lesson Leaderless replication: quorums, hinted handoff and read repair. With the allocator, far fewer tokens do the job. Fewer is better for its own reasons. The docs say each token adds up to 2 × (RF - 1) neighbours on the ring, and work that touches the whole cluster slows down as tokens multiply. The main example is repair, which compares the copies range by range to find and fix differences.

Fewer tokens also fail better. Cassandra 4.0 cut the default from 256 to 16, and The Last Pickle, a company that runs Cassandra clusters for others, measured why. It used six nodes with three copies of every row, read at LOCAL_QUORUM, which means two of each row's three copies must answer. It stopped the same two nodes in each test. With one token per node, all the data could still be read. With three tokens per node, 33.3% of it couldn't.

Why would more tokens hurt? Every arc has its own set of three copies, found by the walk in the stepper. With few arcs per node, a node shares arcs with only a few neighbours, and two dead nodes that aren't neighbours share no arc. With many arcs per node, almost every pair of nodes shares some arc. Then losing any two nodes leaves some rows with only one copy, one short of the two answers a read needs. More tokens even out the load, and raise the odds that two failures make some data unreadable.

The copies come from that same walk. With replication factor 3, the first copy goes to the node owning the first token at or after the key's token. The next copies go to the next different nodes clockwise. NetworkTopologyStrategy, the setting the docs recommend for every real cluster, also spreads the copies over racks, the cabinets of machines that share power and network cables. And it lets each data centre, each building full of machines, keep its own number of copies.

The Try it reads this off a real three-node cluster. A-1001's token falls just before one of cass3's tokens, so cass3 holds the first copy. The next token clockwise is cass1's. The one after that is cass3's again and gets skipped, and the next is cass2's. nodetool getendpoints prints the same three nodes in the same order.

Not every store shows you its tokens. DynamoDB, a database that Amazon runs for its customers, hashes the partition key too, but decides where partitions start and end by itself. It splits a partition that grows too big, and also one that gets too busy, which its 2022 paper calls split for consumption. Bigtable, Google's store from the Data models track, and HBase, a free program built on its design, don't hash at all. They keep keys in order and split ranges by size, as Splitting data showed. That keeps range scans cheap, and sends every time-ordered insert to the last range.

Next, we'll meet the kind of busy that no split and no token can help.

try.title: Find A-1001's replicas on a three-node ring
steps: From the labs folder, start the three-node cluster: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml up -d --wait. It starts one node at a time, which takes about 3 to 4 minutes, and needs about 3 GB of Docker's memory.

Load a small table with three copies of every row: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-06-balances.cql. Find each node's network address with docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 hostname -i (then the same for cass2 and cass3).
Print the ring: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool ring. nodetool is Cassandra's tool for looking inside a running node. Count the lines for each address.

Get the rows' tokens: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 cqlsh -e "SELECT account_id, token(account_id) FROM payments.balances;". Find A-1001's token in the ring printout, and write down the three nodes you expect to hold it.

Check: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool getendpoints payments balances A-1001. When you're done, stop the cluster with docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml down -v. Lessons 5 and 6 start it again.

sections.h: The ring spreads keys, not requests: one busy shop
sections.html:
It's 12:00 on Black Friday, the busiest shopping day of the year in many countries, and shop M-0042 takes 4,000 payments a second, a fifth of all traffic. (The code calls a shop a merchant.) The payments table lives in DynamoDB. In DynamoDB single-table design and transactions, it got a second copy of each payment, sorted by shop. That copy is a global secondary index, or GSI, named byMerchant, and its partition key is the shop's id. So all 4,000 index writes a second carry the same partition key. Everything with one partition key lives in one partition. AWS, Amazon's business that runs DynamoDB, caps a partition at 1,000 write units a second, which is 1,000 writes of items up to 1 KB. About 3,000 of those writes a second are throttled: refused, with an error that says to try again later. It doesn't matter how much capacity the whole table has.

Virtual nodes don't help. They balance keys across nodes, and this is one key. Splitting doesn't help either. The 2022 DynamoDB paper says a partition with heavy traffic on a single item, or one whose keys are written in order, won't benefit from a split. The Dynamo paper assumed this problem away, counting on "enough keys in the popular end of the distribution". A Black Friday shop is one key.

This is also where the pizza picture breaks. A slice measures how many keys a machine holds. It says nothing about how often people ask for one of them, and one key can be most of the asking.

So first, find the busy keys. Count requests per partition key per second, and compare each count with the limit for one partition; the lab builds that counter. In a real system, you don't write it yourself. CloudWatch Contributor Insights, a monitoring feature for DynamoDB, reports the most used and most throttled keys of a table or a GSI. Cassandra's nodetool toppartitions samples the busiest partitions on a node.

Then spread a busy key over several keys. That's write sharding: write M-0042's payments under MERCH#M-0042#0 to MERCH#M-0042#9, choosing the last digit from the payment. The AWS docs describe two ways to choose it. A random suffix spreads best, but then nobody can find one payment's shard again. A suffix worked out from something you know, here hash(paymentId) mod 10, spreads almost as well and can be worked out again for a lookup. Pick the count from numbers: 4,000 writes a second, at 1,000 per partition, needs at least 4 shards. Ten leaves room for a bigger peak. The demo below gets a busiest shard of 454 writes.

The bill moves to the reading side. The third question on that lesson's list, AP3, was "M-0042's FAILED payments since 09:00". It's now 10 queries, one per shard, and your code merges their answers by time. A read that asks many places and merges the answers is a scatter-gather read, and it's the price of the write fix. Pay it only for keys that are really busy.

A key that's read too often is a different problem with a different fix. Say every card payment reads M-0042's settings item. That one item is capped at 3,000 read units a second, where one read unit is one up-to-date read of an item up to 4 KB. A read that may be slightly out of date, an eventually consistent read, costs half a unit, so that's 6,000 small reads. Beyond that, keep a copy in a cache, a fast store of saved answers. DynamoDB Accelerator is Amazon's cache in front of DynamoDB, and Redis, the in-memory store from the Caching track, works too. Don't shard it.

So far we've only counted keys. Moving them copies real bytes, and requests keep arriving while it happens.

try.title: Watch one merchant overload one node, then shard it
steps: Read HotKeyDemo.kt. It puts six nodes on a well-balanced ring (256 tokens each), then sends one second of Black Friday writes: 20,000 payments over 2,000 shops, with M-0042 taking 4,000. It counts writes per node and per key, first keyed by shop, then with a shard suffix worked out from the payment's id.
Predict the busiest node's count in each case, and the busiest key's.

code.title: HotKeyDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l02.demo /** Black Friday: one merchant takes a fifth of all payments. Spread the KEYS evenly, and see what happens to the LOAD. */ fun main() { val nodes = (1..6).map { "node-$it" } val tokens = ring(nodes, 256) // a well-balanced ring: every node owns close to 1/6 fun owner(key: String) = (tokens.ceilingEntry(position(key)) ?: tokens.firstEntry()).value // one second of writes: 20,000 payments over 2,000 merchants, but M-0042 takes 4,000 of them val payments = (0 until 20_000).map { i -> (if (i % 5 == 0) "M-0042" else "M-%04d".format(1_000 + i % 1_999)) to "pay-$i" } fun report(title: String, keyOf: (String, String) -> String) { val perKey = payments.groupingBy { (m, p) -> keyOf(m, p) }.eachCount() val perNode = payments.groupingBy { (m, p) -> owner(keyOf(m, p)) }.eachCount().toSortedMap() val hottest = perKey.maxBy { it.value } println(title) println(" writes per node: $perNode") println(" busiest key: ${hottest.key} with ${hottest.value} writes; keys over 1,000: ${perKey.count { it.value > 1_000 }}") } report("partition key MERCH#<merchant>:") { m, _ -> "MERCH#$m" } // write sharding: a suffix calculated from the payment id, 0 to 9 report("partition key MERCH#<merchant>#<shard of 10>:") { m, p -> "MERCH#$m#${Math.floorMod(position(p), 10L)}" } }

try.expect:
partition key MERCH#<merchant>:
  writes per node: {node-1=2553, node-2=2778, node-3=6777, node-4=2489, node-5=2906, node-6=2497}
  busiest key: MERCH#M-0042 with 4000 writes; keys over 1,000: 1
partition key MERCH#<merchant>#<shard of 10>:
  writes per node: {node-1=3557, node-2=2712, node-3=3206, node-4=2828, node-5=2821, node-6=4876}
  busiest key: MERCH#M-0042#5 with 454 writes; keys over 1,000: 0

The ring is nearly perfect, and node-3 still takes 6,777 writes while the others take about 2,500, because one key can't be split across nodes. After sharding, no key is over 1,000. The nodes are more even, but not perfectly: ten shards land on six nodes, and node-6 drew more than its share of them. The limit per key is the one that throttles, and that one is fixed.

opening:
Six friends share a round pizza. Each one makes a single cut wherever they like, and takes the slice that ends at their own cut. Random cuts sound fair, since nobody chose where anyone else would cut. Then the slices come out, and they're nothing like equal.

The payments company is about to do the same with its machines. Splitting data: key ranges, hashes and tenants placed payments with hash mod N, and ended on the day N changes, when most payments have to move. A ring of hash values moves far fewer. But give each machine one random place on the ring, and its share is a random slice of pizza.

It's easy to trust a hash to be fair, because it spread 10,000 payments over 8 shards almost perfectly. Thousands of keys average out. Six places don't.

In this lesson, we'll build the ring, even it out, read the real one inside Cassandra, a database built on it, and meet the one problem no ring can fix. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with six friends, a pizza cut six times at random, and a ring that gave one machine 44% of the payments. Sixteen cuts each, placed with care, give everyone about a fair slice. But one shop on Black Friday is one slice, and no cutting splits it.

When tickets for a popular concert go on sale, many ticket sites show a waiting page. Thousands of people are asking about one event at once. Ask which one key that crowd is hitting, and how you'd split it.

Next, we'll copy real data when a machine joins, and find out how a request still finds a payment that moved a minute ago.

compare.title: Range partitioning and hash partitioning

a.label: Range (Bigtable, HBase)
a.title: Range (Bigtable, HBase)
a.html:
keys stay sorted; the store cuts them into ranges by size
  tablet 1: ACCT#A-0000 .. ACCT#A-3332
  tablet 2: ACCT#A-3333 .. ACCT#A-6665
  tablet 3: ACCT#A-6666 .. ACCT#A-9999

scan ACCT#A-1000 .. ACCT#A-1999   -> one tablet, already in order
keys that grow with time           -> every new write hits the last range

b.label: Hash (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
b.title: Hash (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
b.html:
token = murmur3(partition key); 16 tokens per node
  A-1001 -> -4994511478997274402
  A-2002 ->  1517767796525818520
  M-0042 ->  5210081981202411406

scan A-1000 .. A-1999   -> every node; no order between partitions
order exists only inside one partition, by the sort key

compare.note: Range partitioning keeps neighbouring keys together, so a range scan is cheap, and it splits a range when it grows. Bigtable and HBase work this way. Its weak spot is any key that grows with time: every insert lands at the end. Hash partitioning scatters neighbouring keys on purpose, so writes spread whatever their keys look like, but a scan across partitions has to ask every node. Cassandra and DynamoDB take both: hash the partition key to choose the place, then keep rows sorted inside it. Neither protects you from a single busy key.

worked.title: Shard M-0042's shop index for Black Friday

steps.say: Start from numbers, not a guess. Last year's peak for M-0042 was 4,000 payments a second. Each index item is about 600 bytes, and writes are counted in steps of 1 KB, rounded up, so each write costs 1 write unit. One partition takes 1,000 a second.
steps.code:
peak writes        4,000 / s     (M-0042 at 12:00 on Black Friday)
write units each   1             (600-byte item, rounded up to 1 KB)
per partition      1,000 / s
minimum shards     4,000 / 1,000 = 4
chosen             10            (room for 2.5x last year's peak)

steps.say: On the writing side, give every payment a shard number worked out from its payment id. The same payment always lands on the same shard, and a lookup can work the number out again. Since late 2025, a DynamoDB GSI can take a key made of several attributes, so a new shop index can use (merchantId, shard) as its partition key. With a key of one attribute, you'd write MERCH#M-0042#3 into a single attribute, as the lab does.
steps.code: fun shardOf(paymentId: String): Int = // the same id always gives the same shard; ids spread evenly over 0..9 Math.floorMod(HashRing.position(paymentId), 10L).toInt() // the payment item from the Data models track's single-table lesson, plus the attribute the sharded index is keyed on val item = Keys.paymentItem(p) + mapOf("shard" to Keys.n(shardOf(p.paymentId).toLong()))

steps.say: On the reading side, AP3 becomes a scatter-gather: one query per shard, all sent at once, then a merge by time. Each shard is asked for the full page size, because the newest 50 could all sit on one shard.
steps.code: suspend fun failedPayments(merchantId: String, from: Instant, limit: Int): List<Payment> = coroutineScope { (0 until 10) .map { shard -> async(Dispatchers.IO) { queryShard(merchantId, shard, "FAILED", from, limit) } } .awaitAll() // 10 Queries in flight at once .flatten() .sortedByDescending { it.createdAt } // merge: newest first across shards .take(limit) }

steps.say: Check the bill against the win. Writes now spread over ten partition keys. Reads of AP3 cost ten requests instead of one, and up to ten times the items. That's the right trade for M-0042 at its peak, and the wrong one for the 1,999 shops that never come near 1,000 a second. So shard only the keys your numbers say are busy.
steps.code:
one key          10 shards
busiest key at peak    4,000 / s        about 450 / s
throttled writes       about 3,000 / s  none
AP3 requests           1                10, in parallel
AP3 items read         limit            up to 10 x limit

lab.title: Build a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes, then catch a hot key
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. Twelve of thirteen fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's error for code that isn't written yet. The one about hash mod S uses the given modOwner and passes.

In HashRing.kt, write addNode (one loop) and ownerOf (one TreeMap lookup, plus the wrap past the top of the ring). The tests on owning, joining and removing pass. Watch the one that checks that a joining node takes keys from one neighbour with one token, and from several with sixteen.
Write preferenceList: walk the tokens clockwise from the key's position, wrapping round once, and keep different nodes until you have n. The test compares yours with a slow walk over every token.
In HotKeys.kt, write HotKeyDetector.record and hotKeys, then WriteSharding.shardKey. All thirteen pass.
Experiment: in the last test of HotKeysTest, change the shard count from 10 to 3 and run it again. 4,000 writes over 3 keys is still more than 1,000 per key, and the test says so. Put it back.
hints: tokens.ceilingEntry(position(key)) is the first token at or after the key, or null past the top of the ring. ?: tokens.firstEntry() wraps round to the start.

For the walk, tokens.tailMap(position(key), true).values is the rest of the ring clockwise, and tokens.values is the whole ring from the bottom. Chain the two as sequences and stop as soon as you have enough. A LinkedHashSet keeps the order and ignores repeats.
Ask for n copies on a ring of 2 nodes and you can only get 2: stop at minOf(n, nodes.size).
The second of a timestamp is Math.floorDiv(atMillis, 1000L). HashMap.merge(key, 1, Int::plus) counts, and merge(key, n, ::maxOf) keeps a maximum.
Positions can be negative, so position(paymentId) % 10 can be negative too. Math.floorMod can't.
lab.done: All thirteen tests in HashRingTest and HotKeysTest pass.

drill.title: The ring lookup and the replica walk from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a Kotlin function owner(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long): String, and a function replicas(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long, n: Int): List<String> that returns n different nodes clockwise from the key. Then say in one sentence why replicas has to skip some tokens.

answer.html: fun owner(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long): String = // the first token at or after the key; past the top of the ring, wrap to the first token (tokens.ceilingEntry(keyPosition) ?: tokens.firstEntry()).value fun replicas(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long, n: Int): List<String> { val want = minOf(n, tokens.values.toSet().size) val found = LinkedHashSet<String>() // clockwise from the key to the top, then from the bottom: each token at most once for (node in tokens.tailMap(keyPosition, true).values.asSequence() + tokens.values.asSequence()) { found += node if (found.size == want) break } return found.toList() } // With virtual nodes, the next tokens often belong to a node already on the list, // and two copies on one machine are lost together when it dies.

recap: With one random token per node, shares are very uneven: about 41% for the luckiest of six nodes, against a fair 16.7%.

Virtual nodes give each node many tokens, so its share is a sum of small arcs and lands near the average. Random tokens need many per node, which is why Cassandra 5.0 pairs num_tokens: 16 with a token allocator.

A joining node takes the slice before each of its tokens: with many tokens, small slices from several nodes, and a dead node's load spreads the same way. The walk for copies skips tokens of nodes already chosen. Rendezvous and jump hashing move the same fair share with no ring.

More tokens balance the load, but make it likelier that two failed nodes leave some rows unreadable. Cassandra hashes the partition key with Murmur3, and token() and nodetool getendpoints show where a row lives.

The limit: the ring balances keys, not requests. One busy partition key is capped at 1,000 writes and 3,000 reads a second in DynamoDB. Count requests per key, shard busy writes with a worked-out suffix and merge on read, and cache busy reads.

explain.prompt: A teammate is planning a six-node Cassandra cluster and asks two things. Why do we need 16 tokens per node instead of one? And will that also save us when M-0042 does 4,000 payments a second on Black Friday? Answer both.
explain.answer: With one token per node, each node owns the single arc that ends at its token, and six random points cut a circle very unevenly. The luckiest node owns about 41% of the ring on average, so it stores and answers about 41% of everything. When a node joins, it takes its whole share from one neighbour, and when one dies, one neighbour inherits all its work. With many tokens per node, each node owns many small arcs, so the shares even out. A joining node then takes small slices from several nodes at once, and a dead node's work spreads over many. Cassandra 5.0 uses 16 tokens and an allocator that places them on purpose for three copies, because random tokens need hundreds per node to even out, and every token makes repair and copying slower. None of that helps M-0042. Tokens balance keys, and M-0042's payments share one partition key, so they all hit one partition and its copies. For that we shard the key, for example the shop's id plus a suffix from 0 to 9 worked out from the payment id, and the shop's screen merges the ten partitions when it reads.

deeper.html:
Dynamo's paper, section 6.2, tells how Amazon changed its way of dividing the ring while the system was in use, and its three strategies make a good map of the choices. T is tokens per node, S is the number of nodes, and Q is a fixed number of equal partitions.

Strategy Tokens Partitions Problem it had or fixed
1 T random tokens per node ranges between tokens filling a new node took almost a day; the Merkle trees (hash summaries used to compare copies) had to be rebuilt whenever ranges changed
2 T random tokens per node Q equal-sized ranges separated where data sits from how it's divided; the worst balance, used only during the move between 1 and 3
3 Q/S tokens per node Q equal-sized ranges the best balance in their measurements; a partition moves as one file, so filling and archiving got simpler

Strategy 3's price, in the paper's words, is that changing the membership needs coordination to keep the assignment right. Cassandra's token allocator works on the same problem from the other side: it keeps the number of tokens per node fixed and chooses where the new ones go.

The 2022 DynamoDB paper tells the other half: how the service learned to live with busy partitions. At first each partition got a fixed share of the throughput the table had paid for, and splitting a partition for size divided that share, so a table could be throttled while mostly idle. DynamoDB added bursting (unused capacity saved for up to 300 seconds), then adaptive capacity (boosting the partitions being throttled). It then replaced both with global admission control, which tracks a table's use across all its request routers. Split for consumption came on top: a partition that gets too busy is split at a point chosen from the keys it has seen. The paper's own limit is the one this lesson ends on: a single busy item, or a key range written in order, can't be helped by a split.

To see the 2 × (RF - 1) neighbours rule, list the token ranges a node is responsible for with nodetool describering payments on the three-node cluster. With 16 tokens per node, each node copies and repairs dozens of ranges instead of three.
